title: Playing with Armstrong versus Ellington: freedom and cliques
summary: Bigard preferred Armstrong's small band because he could play as many bars as he wished, while Duke's big band confined solos to eight or sixteen bars and had cliques.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: I know that later in your career you worked with Louig Armstrong. What about the difference in the music of Armstrong and Ellington?

Well, that's two different styles of music, to begin with. And Ellington has got a large band, Louie had a seven piece band, which -- and, to be truthful, I enjoyed both bands but I enjoyed Louig's more because I had more freedom in my playing, where Duke, you got to play what you see on the paper plus what you would say freedom, but it wasn't that much freedom. It doesn't give you a chance to even concentrate on really what you want to do because it's so short.
Yeah, that's what I'm saying. It comes within like eight bars, 16 bars, and that's it. But

with Armstrong you can play as many bars as you want because -- it doesn't bother you -- he doesn't bother you. The little band doesn't bother you. In other words, they tried to help you, to push you along, because they realized that they're small and every man counts. You know, it means something for each guy in the group where --
How was the spirit of the members of the band in Ellington compared with Armstrong's? The feelings of the men for the music and each other (unintelligible)?

Oh, I guess the feeling was all right. But I think that they were more close in Louis's aggregation because it's smaller, where Duke's is larger and they go like -- I hate to say that -- I mean, like cliques. Each band got cliques in the band. You know, like certain guys go with certain guys. But Armstrong's band's too small for that kind of business. You know what I mean.
Was there a competitive feeling in Duke's band among the men?
Oh, I don't think so. I mean, I think it could be a little jealousy feeling, that sometime -- but I don't think they thought about being competitive or nothing like that.
No, you don't have time to think about anything like that with Louis. I mean, he was wonderful.
